title: Flea-Borne Typhus Outbreak Hits L.A. Neighborhood as County Cases Hit Record
excerpt: Los Angeles County health officials are investigating a localized typhus outbreak in Pico-Union after five residents were hospitalized, part of a record 220-case year countywide.
body:
• Los Angeles County health officials are investigating a localized flea-borne typhus outbreak in the Pico-Union neighborhood, where five residents fell ill this year and all were hospitalized before recovering.
  • The county recorded a record 220 typhus cases in 2025, up from 187 in 2024, with nearly nine in ten patients requiring hospitalization.
  • The disease spreads through infected flea feces — carried by rats, opossums and free-roaming cats — and is not transmitted person to person. It is treatable with antibiotics when caught early.
  • Officials urge year-round flea control for pets, avoiding stray and wild animals, and securing trash that attracts rodents.

A once-uncommon disease is resurfacing in Los Angeles neighborhoods. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health is investigating a localized outbreak of flea-borne typhus in Pico-Union, where five residents fell ill this year — every one of them sick enough to be hospitalized. All five have recovered, county officials said, but the cluster is a warning sign in a year that has already become the county's worst on record for the disease.

The Pico-Union cases are not tied to a single address, officials noted, and the investigation there is unfolding alongside a separate cluster in downtown Los Angeles. Both fit a broader and more troubling pattern: Los Angeles County logged a record 220 cases of flea-borne typhus in 2025, the highest number ever recorded in the county and up from 187 cases in 2024. County data show cases have been rising almost every year since 2010, when just 31 were reported.

A severe illness hiding in plain sight

Flea-borne typhus is a bacterial infection caused by Rickettsia typhi and R. felis, carried in infected fleas and their feces. Fleas reach people through rats, free-roaming cats and opossums — not from person to person. Infection typically occurs when flea feces enter the body through small cuts in the skin or are rubbed into the eyes, often around the home when pets or wildlife carry fleas indoors.

Symptoms appear one to two weeks after exposure and include high fever, headache, chills, body aches, a characteristic rash, and nausea or vomiting. What makes the disease dangerous is how quickly it escalates: in 2025, nearly nine in ten people diagnosed in Los Angeles County required hospitalization, with patients ranging in age from 1 to 85.

"As flea-borne typhus cases continue to increase across Los Angeles County, preventing exposure to infected fleas is more important than ever."

— Muntu Davis, Los Angeles County Health Officer

The illness is treatable — doxycycline and other antibiotics work well when the infection is caught early, and prompt treatment brings the fatality rate below 1 percent. But because the early symptoms mimic flu and other common infections, diagnosis often comes late, which helps explain the high hospitalization rate.

Why cases keep climbing

Public health records point beyond fleas to the environmental cycle that sustains them: rodents, free-roaming animals, accumulated trash, food sources, vegetation, animal harborage — and, in some areas, homeless encampments. County surveillance shows clusters concentrated in Central and South Los Angeles, and officials have previously declared parts of downtown, including Skid Row, typhus zones when conditions deteriorated.

The county is working with the city of Los Angeles on environmental safety measures to reduce transmission, and continues to monitor confirmed outbreak zones. Warm weather extends flea season, and mosquito season — which runs roughly June through November — overlaps with the period of highest typhus activity.

What residents can do

The health department's guidance is practical and household-level: keep pets on flea control year-round, avoid touching or feeding stray and wild animals — especially opossums, rats and feral cats — store trash in cans with secure lids, and clear crawl spaces, attics and areas under decks where rats and strays shelter. Anyone who might have been exposed and develops fever, headache or a rash should seek medical care promptly and mention the possible exposure.

For Los Angeles County's large South Asian community — with pet-owning, multigenerational households concentrated from Artesia's Little India to the San Fernando Valley — the takeaway is straightforward: year-round flea prevention for pets costs far less than a hospital stay, and the disease responds well to early treatment. Five hospitalizations in Pico-Union is a small cluster, but the record 220 cases countywide suggest the risk is no longer confined to any one neighborhood.
